attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay, stated as his view.

semantics.note: A firm retrospective causal claim. The proposition lists poor quality and the attitude shift side by side and drops the 'mostly because' link, but the contract puts that link back. The language is hyperbolic but not hedged.

contract.note: An ordinary plain reading: 'millions' as at least two million, 'radicalized' as a substantial negative shift in attitude, and performance as the main cause. It requires population-level causal evidence, which suits the size of the claim. It is not stretched against the speaker.

evidence.note: A Dec 2024 survey of how much value users see in phone AI features. It measures apathy, not changes in attitude toward AI caused by Apple.
US polling shows AI skepticism rising through June 2025 but does not link it to Apple Intelligence.
Morgan Stanley survey (via PYMNTS) finding a favorable reception among iPhone owners. It weighs against the claim but cannot rule out a negatively affected subgroup of millions.

reviews.rationale: No representative or longitudinal evidence counts people whose general views on AI worsened mainly because of Apple Intelligence. e1 and e2 show product apathy and wider skepticism. e3 shows a fairly favorable reception. None of the three meets the support or the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, answering the ASIC counterargument he raises himself.

semantics.note: A firm conditional ('it still fucks up') with an antecedent ('if this actually happens') that refers to ASICs replacing GPU spending. In context, 'this' may mean OpenAI's chip specifically. The drafter's broader reading is reasonable.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as material substitution of ASICs for NVIDIA GPUs fits the context about cutting GPU spend. Adoption alone is rightly not counted. 'Damage' has no stated measure, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: An AWS disclosure that about 500k Trainium2 chips were in service by Nov 2025. This shows ASIC adoption, not displacement of NVIDIA purchases.
NVIDIA's Q2 FY27 release shows strong Data Center growth. It is a company disclosure and does not address the counterfactual effect of substitution.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent, material substitution of ASICs for NVIDIA GPUs, is not established: e1 shows adoption only. A conditional with an unknown antecedent is not scored. NVIDIA's continued growth (e2) cannot refute an undated consequence, and no attributable damage is shown.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: A firm, undated forecast ('at some point... will'). The cost cut follows the slowdown. 'Have to come down' is framed as a necessity, not a hedge. The proposition keeps the 'such as generative AI' scope.

contract.note: Treating any quarter-over-quarter dip in YoY revenue growth as 'slowing' sets a low bar for the antecedent, but the contract still requires slowdown-caused cuts to gen-AI spending and does not let elapsed time count as a contradiction. Fair overall.

evidence.note: Meta Q2 2026 revenue growth of 28%, a baseline for the slowdown. It is not evidence of the predicted cut.
Meta Q3 2026 growth slowed to 26%, but capex rose and the release gives no sign of gen-AI cuts. This meets the antecedent but not the outcome.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's reading, Meta's growth slowed (28% to 26%), but no evidence shows a cut to separately measured, loss-making gen-AI spending caused by that slowdown. Capex actually rose. With no deadline, continued spending cannot contradict the forecast, so it remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own conclusion drawn from the Cursor story.

semantics.note: Combines a present-tense characterization ('biggest threats') with a firm dispositional 'will rent-seek and punish'. Under the policy, 'will' makes it a forecast. The hyperbole ('loot') is rightly dropped from the proposition.

contract.note: Reading the claim as exploitation of successful customers plus a comparative 'biggest threat' is ordinary. Excluding routine price changes and requiring conduct by both firms is reasonable. Because the key terms are undefined, interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Anthropic restricted subscription use of third-party tools from Apr 2026, citing capacity and its terms of service. This is not shown to be punishment of a successful business customer.

OpenAI's proposed end of its Cursor agreement was triggered by a change of control after the SpaceX acquisition, not by Cursor's success. The cutoff falls after the evaluation date. Context, not support.
Windsurf's July 16, 2025 update says access was restored. This predates the statement and cannot settle later conduct.

reviews.rationale: Neither firm is shown exploiting customers because of their success. Anthropic's restriction cites capacity, and OpenAI's withdrawal cites change of control and was only proposed. No comparative evidence addresses 'biggest threat'. With no deadline and no decisive event either way, the forecast is unresolved.
